habitat: Sumatran tigers inhabit the tropical forests, peat swamps, and freshwater swamp forests of the Indonesian island of Sumatra. They are found in both lowland and montane forest regions, from sea level to elevations above 3,000 meters. Their habitat is characterized by dense vegetation, high rainfall, and a rich ecosystem of prey species. Rapid deforestation for palm oil plantations has severely reduced their available range, confining them to increasingly fragmented pockets of forest.
diet: Sumatran tigers are obligate carnivores, hunting wild boar, sambar and barking deer, pig-tailed macaques, fish, birds, and occasionally small elephants and rhino calves. They are ambush predators, using their distinctive striped coat for camouflage in the dappled forest light. A single tiger may consume up to 18 kilograms of meat in one feeding and can survive several days between kills. In areas where natural prey is scarce, tigers may prey on livestock, bringing them into conflict with humans.
behavior: Sumatran tigers are solitary and territorial, with males maintaining territories of 60-100 square kilometers and females 20-40 square kilometers. They are primarily nocturnal hunters but may be active at any time. These tigers are excellent swimmers and readily cross rivers and swamps within their range. Females give birth to 2-3 cubs after a gestation period of approximately 103 days, and cubs remain with their mother for up to two years, learning essential hunting and survival skills.
facts: The Sumatran tiger is the smallest surviving tiger subspecies, with males weighing 100-140 kg and females 75-110 kg. They have the darkest coat and narrowest stripes of all tigers, excellent camouflage for the dense jungle environment. Fewer than 400 Sumatran tigers remain in the wild, making them critically endangered. Unlike other tiger subspecies, Sumatran tigers have webbing between their toes, helping them swim efficiently through their swampy habitat.
naming: Sumatran-inspired names reflect their jungle environment and powerful nature. Consider names meaning 'striped,' 'forest,' or 'powerful' in Indonesian: Harimau (tiger in Indonesian), Rimba (jungle), Api (fire — for their orange coat), Bayang (shadow), Belang (stripe), Guntur (thunder), Intan (diamond), or Kuat (strong).
